# Subagent contract

Injected into every subagent by the `SubagentStart` hook (`.claude/hooks/pf-subagent-context.py`).
A subagent launches with an empty context — it does not inherit `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`, the
parent's conversation, or anything the parent learned. This file is the only project law it sees, so
it repeats what matters instead of pointing at a document you cannot read.

This half is the framework's (`docs/framework/SUBAGENTS.md`, overwritten by every agent-doc sync). A
SKU adds its own rules in a repo-root `SUBAGENTS.md` using the same `<!-- profile: NAME -->`
markers; the hook appends each of its sections after the framework's.

<!-- profile: all -->

## Round-trip discipline

Every turn re-sends your whole context to the model, so one extra **turn** costs far more than one
extra tool **call** inside a turn. N inspections in N turns bill that context N times. Batch by
dependency, not by habit.

- **Every independent shell command goes in ONE call through `Tools/pf/pf-exec`** — it is the batched
  SHELL door, not an inspection tool. Reads and greps, but equally `dotnet build`, `dotnet test`, a
  gate script, a `git` query. A heredoc of `label : command` lines, run in parallel, **each result
  capped**, and a failing item never aborts the others. Measured on a SKU: an exploration that ran as
  **26 separate model calls** was 26 independent commands — two `pf-exec` calls. Parallel `Bash`
  calls in one message save the same turns but cap nothing, so prefer `pf-exec` whenever output size
  is uncertain. Ordered shell — build, then test, then gate — is `--ordered --stop-on-fail --reduce auto`.

  ```
  Tools/pf/pf-exec --cap 3k <<'EOF'
  spec    : read _bmad-output/planning-artifacts/epics.md:1200-1260
  sig     : rg -n "class SomeModel" Assets
  callers : rg -n "SomeFactory" Assets -l
  EOF
  ```

  **It exists and it runs — do not verify it.** No `ls`, no `--help`, no reading its source, no "let
  me check the syntax first": that is a whole model turn spent on a tool this contract just handed
  you. Call it. If the shell ever says command not found, that one failed call is your answer and you
  fall back to several `Bash` calls in one message.

  `read FILE:L1-L2` replaces a `Read` call. Items are marked `EMPTY` / `TRUNCATED n->m` / `exit N`;
  when a cut mattered, rerun that one item alone with a bigger `--cap`.
- **Two single reads in a row is a smell; the third is a defect.** Before the second one, ask what
  else you already know you need and send the whole set at once. A turn that spends several calls is
  the goal — fewer reads is not.
- **Never `Read` a large file whole** — the host truncates at 25k tokens and hands you a pagination
  notice, so you pay for the blob *and* for the extra turns. Locate first with `rg -n`, **then put
  every slice you now know you need into one `pf-exec`** — grep-then-slice is only cheaper than the
  blob if the slices arrive together.
- **Never batch across a dependency.** Do not guess the output of a compile, a test run, or a file you
  have not read yet. When the next call's input depends on this call's result, take the extra turn —
  that is what turns are for.
- **Read a file once.** Do not re-read what you wrote yourself.

## Where files are, and where they are not

- **Never run `find /`, or any search rooted above the project directory** — it costs minutes and
  answers nothing.
- A framework type → `docs/framework/framework-api.index.json`; its `file` values are relative to the
  **package root**: `Packages/com.classicspins.prototype-framework/` if that folder exists; otherwise
  the `file:` path `Packages/manifest.json` declares for the package (already the root — never append
  `pathPrefix`); otherwise the newest `Library/PackageCache/com.classicspins.prototype-framework@*`.
- A third-party package's source is `Library/PackageCache/<package-id>@*` — read it, never edit it.
- `Library/ScriptAssemblies`, `Library/Bee`, `Temp/`, `Logs/`, `obj/` are build output: never read
  them. `.meta` files are source; read one only to resolve a GUID.

## Reporting

Report `path:line` plus a one-line finding each. No code dumps, no file contents pasted back — the
parent pays for your report in its own context.

<!-- profile: readonly -->

## You are read-only

Modify nothing — not through `Write`/`Edit`, and not through `Bash`. No `pf-write`, no `sed -i`, no
`>`/`>>` into a repo file, no `git` command that writes. If a task seems to need a write, stop and
report it as a finding instead.

<!-- profile: mutating -->

## Put every write you already know you need in ONE message

Your host runs as many `Write` and `Edit` calls as a single assistant message carries, all of them,
before it calls you again. Six files created together cost **one** turn; six files created one per
step cost **six**, and each of those six re-sends your whole context. Measured on a SKU: the same
six-file task costs **47k context tokens batched against 330k one-at-a-time**.

So decide the whole set first, then emit it:

```
(one message)   Write A.cs   Write B.cs   Write C.cs   Write D.cs
```

Only a write whose content depends on a result you have not seen yet — a compile, a test run, a file
you have not read — earns its own turn. That one is a real dependency; the rest are habit.

**Write deliverables straight to their final path.** The scratchpad is for genuinely throwaway things:
a diff, a note, an ops file you are about to pipe. Drafting real files there and copying them into the
repo afterwards doubles every write.

## `Tools/pf/pf-write` — for the batch that must not half-apply

Not for batching as such; the message above already does that. Use it when several files have to land
together or not at all.

```
Tools/pf/pf-write <<'EOF'
[ {"op":"edit","path":"Assets/A.cs","old":"var x = 1;","new":"var x = 2;"},
  {"op":"write","path":"Assets/C.cs","text":"// whole file\n"},
  {"op":"delete","path":"Assets/Old.cs"} ]
EOF
```

JSON, so nothing you write can collide with a delimiter. **All-or-nothing, the opposite of
`pf-exec`:** every item is validated before anything is touched, and a failure mid-apply rolls the
whole tree back. `edit` needs exactly `count` occurrences (default 1) and refuses an ambiguous match
rather than guessing. `--dry-run` validates without writing. Group the edits you already know you
need; an edit whose content depends on a test result you have not seen yet is not one of them.

## Unity and compile

- **Type-check in the shell before you refresh Unity.** `Tools/pf/typecheck-headless.sh` (pure C#),
  `Tools/pf/typecheck.sh <Asm>`, `Tools/pf/typecheck.sh --changed`. A `dotnet build` error is one
  Bash turn; the same error found through `assets-refresh` + `console-get-logs` costs a domain reload,
  an MCP round trip, and a log payload you carry for the rest of the session.
- **Drive the Editor through `Tools/pf/pf-mcp`** — ordered calls, payload reduced in the shell,
  screenshots returned as a path. Never call `console-get-logs` unfiltered.
- **Never edit anything under `Packages/` or `Library/PackageCache`.** Framework code is changed in the
  framework repo, never here.
- **Never run Unity batchmode locally**, and never sweep a content set in play mode.
- **A timed-out call is still running.** A gateway or `pf-timeout` expiry means the Editor is still
  executing what you sent, not that it failed — never re-issue it: the second copy queues behind the
  first on the Editor's single main thread. Any Editor job that can outlast one MCP call (a generator,
  a seed search, a bake) wants an **engine-free door** first — a `dotnet` tool that builds from the same
  source file the menu item uses — and never a synchronous `script-execute`.
- **Keep every tool call under ~4 minutes: your prompt cache lives five.** A call that blocks longer
  lets the cache expire, and your next turn re-writes the whole context at full price. Measured on a
  SKU: one stage agent did this twice (a 729 s batch of 43 per-class `tests-run` items, and one 341 s
  call), re-writing about 510k tokens each time. A turn from a warm cache costs cents.
  - `Tools/pf/pf-mcp` enforces this itself (`--turn-budget 240`). It stops starting items when the
    budget runs out and ends with `INCOMPLETE … continue: Tools/pf/pf-mcp … < FILE`, exit 1. That is
    not a failure. Run exactly that command as your next call, and repeat until no `INCOMPLETE` line
    comes back. Never pass `--turn-budget 0`.
- **Run EditMode tests through `Tools/pf/pf-tests`, never per-class `pf-mcp tests-run`.** It runs any
  set of classes as ONE synchronous Unity run and reads the verdict from a file. An unfocused Editor —
  which is how you always find it — ticks ~6 times a second, so every MCP `tests-run` pays ~8-10 s
  before a single test runs; a 45-class sweep cost 10-13 min where `pf-tests --all` takes under a
  minute.
  - In the loop, name the classes you touched: `Tools/pf/pf-tests MapArtTests MapScreenTests`. That
    takes a few seconds.
  - At the end of the stage, run `Tools/pf/pf-tests --auto` ONCE. That is the fast tier, plus the
    `[Category("Slow")]` capture/floor classes only when your diff touches a path that draws. Report
    which tier ran; the tool prints it.
  - `INCOMPLETE … pf-tests --wait <id>` is the turn budget, not a failure. Run exactly that next.
  - `reused` means the inputs are byte-identical to the last green run of that selection. It is a
    pass. Do not `--rerun` it.
  - One Unity call at a time. A synchronous run holds the Editor's main thread, and pf-tests refuses
    to start a second run while its last one is live.
- **The visual judge is the one allowed long call.** It owns its ceiling (`UIGATE_JUDGE_TIMEOUT`,
  840 s), so run it with the Bash `timeout` set to `900000` and never wrap it in a shorter
  `pf-timeout`. At the JPEG default it answers in about 1-3 minutes. An exit 2 saying "no answer
  within Ns" is a transport failure: report it, do not re-run it under a smaller cap.
